facts: The **top view** (or plan) is what you see looking straight down.
The **front view** is what you see looking straight at the front.
The **side view** is what you see looking from the left or right.
Each view is a flat outline made of squares; hidden cubes behind others are not shown as extra squares.
steps: Choose the direction (top, front or side).
Imagine flattening the object onto that wall or floor.
Draw the outline you would see as a grid of squares.

development.question_text:
A stack has front-view column heights $1,3,2$.
Sketch the front view on a square grid.

mastery.question_text:
Two solids have the same rectangular top view.
One has a rectangular front view and one has a triangular front view.
Explain why the top view alone is not enough to identify them.
mastery.solution_text: The top view hides height and sloping faces. A rectangular prism and a triangular prism can share the same rectangular footprint but have different front views.

mastery.question_text:
A cube stack has top-view cells in an L-shape.
The front-view column heights are $2,1$ and the side-view column heights are $2,1$.
Describe one possible stack.
mastery.solution_text: Place a stack of height $2$ at the corner of the L and one cube in each of the two adjoining cells.

mastery.question_text:
A square pyramid and a triangular prism both have triangular front views.
Name one other view that distinguishes them and explain how.
mastery.solution_text: The top view distinguishes them: the pyramid gives a square with lines to the centre, while the prism gives a rectangle with a ridge line.
